title: The Greenway Exhibit Puzzle
short: A museum-style science exhibit seems to have been secretly replaced.
brief: A fictional outdoor science exhibition inspired by the Yakima Greenway discovers that its brightly colored climate-information panel has changed appearance overnight. A nearby container holds a second panel. Use light exposure, pigment comparison, instrument logs, and witness accounts to determine whether the display was vandalized or temporarily replaced.
caseQuestion: Who swapped the display panel, and what physical evidence distinguishes the two versions?

sites.name: Public exhibit frame
sites.label: Climate display panel
sites.desc: One panel has evenly printed halftone dots instead of irregular paint strokes.

sites.name: Storage alcove
sites.label: Padded display sleeve
sites.desc: An original hand-painted panel is preserved behind a protective cover.

sites.name: Light testing bench

sites.name: Volunteer desk
sites.label: Exhibit change log
sites.desc: The official display change list has no temporary replacement entry.

clues.title: Panel magnification
clues.detail: At magnification, the displayed panel contains regular arrays of tiny printed dots. The archived original has uneven hand-painted pigment boundaries.
clues.question: What does the repeating dot pattern suggest?
options: A printed reproduction
A new naturally growing pigment
A clock-reading error

clues.title: Mounting tabs
clues.detail: The clear frame has no cracks. Its tabs show recent tool-free opening and resealing.
clues.question: What can be inferred?
options: Only vandalism is possible
The frame was opened without breaking it
The color was caused by rainfall alone

clues.title: Protected artwork
clues.detail: The stored panel has unique brush patterns matching the older photograph, and it is safely sealed in a padded sleeve.
clues.question: Why is the matching texture useful?
options: It proves a weather forecast
It identifies a footprint
It links the stored panel to the original display

clues.title: Exposure study
clues.detail: A simulated UV-exposure comparison shows that delicate pigments may change with accumulated light exposure. Actual conservation depends on material and wavelength.
clues.question: Why would a conservator remove an original panel temporarily?
options: To limit unnecessary light exposure
To make a weather station faster
To change a person’s handwriting

clues.title: Replica ink strip
clues.detail: A small printed proof sheet uses the same regular dot pattern and colors as the public panel.
clues.question: Which link does this support?
options: A chemical explosion
The installed panel is likely a printed replica
An exact fingerprint identification

clues.title: Visitor photographs
clues.detail: Two photographs taken one day apart show subtle differences in letter edges but the same overall illustration.
clues.question: What is the reasonable conclusion?
options: The exhibit relocated to another city
A person confessed in writing
Two similar versions may have been shown

clues.title: Missing change entry
clues.detail: The official log still lists the original as on display. A separate conservation note mentions a temporary replica trial.
clues.question: What process should improve?
options: Record substitutions in the shared exhibit log
Keep changes secret to reduce confusion
Destroy older paperwork

labs.title: UV exposure index
labs.story: Adjust relative light intensity and compare a simplified exposure index.
labs.explanation: Higher light intensity raises cumulative exposure in this fixed-time teaching model.
labs.question: Which scientific interpretation is best supported by this model?
options: More light can increase the exposure index.
Light intensity identifies a person.
A photograph measures exact UV dose.

labs.title: Print pattern model
labs.story: Change dot density and observe the number of marks in a fixed sample window.
labs.explanation: Printed dot arrays can be differentiated from irregular paint marks at sufficient magnification.
labs.question: Which scientific interpretation is best supported by this model?
options: A more regular print always uses fewer dots.
Increasing dot density increases dots in a fixed width.
All drawings have perfectly regular dot rows.

labs.title: Shield transmission
labs.story: Adjust shield transmission and estimate light passing through.
labs.explanation: Lower transmission means less modeled light passes through the shield.
labs.question: Which scientific interpretation is best supported by this model?
options: A shield sets the calendar date.
Lower transmission increases the modeled light.
Lower transmission passes less light in this model.

math.prompt: A shield allows 30% of 200 light units through. How many units pass through it?

explanation: Print magnification, the matching protected original, and the conservation note support a temporary unrecorded substitution by the exhibit conservator, rather than proof of vandalism.

witnesses.name: Brynn Kade
witnesses.statement: I had discussed the possibility of using a printed replica during a conservation test. I inspected both display materials.
witnesses.followup: I kept a separate conservation note, but the public display-change log was not yet checked.
witnesses.question: Which physical comparison best tests Brynn’s conservation explanation?
options: Compare print dots with the stored painted panel
Count nearby ducks
Compare the weather in other counties

witnesses.name: Imani Voss
witnesses.statement: I locked the exhibit door after visitor hours. I did not open the display frame.
witnesses.followup: I did see a padded carrying sleeve near the storage alcove.
witnesses.question: How could the guide’s sleeve sighting be checked?
options: Guess what was inside the sleeve
Inspect the sleeve and inventory records
Assume a padded sleeve implies damage

witnesses.name: Felix Brooks
witnesses.statement: I tested two different lamp covers on the demonstration board.
witnesses.followup: The light meter was logged before I left.
witnesses.question: What does Felix’s lighting test not identify?
options: Possible light exposure
An exposure measurement
The person who exchanged the panel

witnesses.name: Dara Wynn
witnesses.statement: I took photographs both afternoons from the same marked location.
witnesses.followup: The smaller title letters looked slightly different in the later photo.
witnesses.question: Which method makes Dara’s photographs useful comparisons?
options: Use similar framing and compare visual details
Ignore the date metadata
Assume all colors are identical

note: Entirely fictional educational case using a real regional place name as setting. No actual person, facility, business, incident, or allegation is represented.
